newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Foreign airlines fly at S.Africa market.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Foreign airlines fly at S.Africa market.

text.p: Competition in South Africa's skies is heating up as foreign airlines taxi in for business, threatening decades of domination by state-owned South African Airways (SAA).

While newcomers like Virgin Atlantic wow passengers with limousine services and on-board massages, the 63-year-old national carrier has recently put to bed a disruptive strike and is bracing itself for an uncertain privatisation process.

Last year two of the world's major carriers took on SAA SAA.CN, both on its money-spinning Johannesburg-London route and on its domestic turf. A new local airline, Air SA, is also expected to start flying to Britain in April, unseating SAA as the only South African carrier on this route.

Virgin set up shop in October, introducing three flights a week between Britain and South Africa, a move that added an additional 1,500 seats a week to the popular route at an initial cut-price launch fare of about $533 return at a time when SAA's cheapest fare was about $823.
Since then Virgin and SAA, which is the largest commercial airline in Africa, have stayed neck-and-neck on pricing with both airlines' cheapest economy fare at 3,390 rand ($726) return for January.
"In the economy cabin we will not allow ourselves to be outpriced by SAA or BA (British Airways)," said David James, Virgin's general manager for southern Africa.
In June British Airways Plc, which already flies the London-Johannesburg route, signed a franchise agreement with South Africa's biggest independent domestic carrier, Comair.

Under this deal Comair, which flies to most major cities in South Africa and the southern African countries alongside SAA, has assumed the British airline's name and livery. BA travellers to South Africa can now book their internal travel on Comair from overseas.
SAA NOT WORRIED BY NEW COMPETITION
Leon Els, senior manager of SAA corporate relations, is non-committal about the impact of the new entrants, saying it is too early to judge what will happen.
On competition from Virgin, he said: "At this stage there has not been a marked decrease in our market share because of the high demand for seats on this route."

However, a better assessment could be made once Virgin doubled its flights to six a week from March 1, Els added. SAA currently flies to London 14 times a week and BA will soon increase its scheduled flights to 15 a week.
Another SAA spokesman estimated SAA's current share of the London route at around 40 percent of total traffic.
Els also said there had not been any negative spin-offs for SAA from the Comair-BA tie up.

SAA estimates its current portion of the market at 65-70 percent, down from 75 percent two years ago. Els attributed the drop to SAA giving up thinner routes to local carrier SA Express, in which SAA has a 49 percent stake.

Piet van Hoven, Comair's managing director, estimates his airline's market share at around 17 percent of the domestic market, compared with about 15 percent at the time of the BA announcement. It has set a target of 35 percent in five years.

Virgin has also moved in on SAA at home with the signing in November of a code-sharing agreement with another local airline, Sun Air, previously the official carrier of the former "homeland" of Bophuthatswana and now owned by the South African government.
PRIVATISATION OF AIRLINES ON CARDS
Virgin plans to buy a stake in Sun Air when the government sells it off next year as part of its privatisation programme.

"We would certainly be looking for a 25 percent stake, which is the limit that foreign companies can take in privatised assets. We hope that the government will relax the restrictions so we can take a greater stake," Virgin's James said.

While international players plan expansion into the local market, SAA has been grappling with a number of problems, not least of all a 10-day strike in October by engineers and technicians that cost the operator more than 40 million rand.

In the six months to September the group plunged to a 75 million rand loss mainly due to a rise in gasoline prices fuelled by a weaker rand. The local currency lost almost 30 percent of its value against the dollar in 1996.
Asked if SAA could bounce back to profit for the full year, Els said: "It is going to be very difficult but we have gone on various cost-saving exercises to lessen the losses."
In the year to March 1996 SAA turned in a profit after finance costs of 324 million rand.

SAA is also on the government's privatisation agenda, seen as the airline's biggest shake-up since deregulation in 1991 before which SAA had a monopoly on main domestic routes. Latest reports from the Public Enterprises Ministry are that SAA will seek a foreign equity partner by the middle of 1998.
SAA SPREADS FOREIGN WINGS, BUT LOCAL PROBLEMS NIGGLE

In other developments SAA has recently shifted its Asian hub from Singapore to Bangkok and begins flying to Japan on April 3. It is also expanding its network of foreign alliances, which includes code share agreements with Germany's Lufthansa and American Airlines. Agreements with Thai Airways and British Midland are also on the cards.
But on the local front relations are strained with Comair. A price war ensued soon after the BA link-up and SAA has accused Comair of spying into its computer database.

SAA has also lodged a formal complaint against the tie-up with the air service licensing authorities on the grounds that the deal allows a foreign carrier to operate an air service in South Africa without the appropriate licence.
